Illinois Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession FAQ

Can a squatter take ownership of my Illinois house?

Check the statute and talk to a Illinois attorney about your facts.

Can a squatter take ownership of an Illinois house?

Only by meeting a statutory test that takes years and includes paying the property taxes. Ownership claims based on occupation come through adverse possession provisions in Article XIII of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the best known one requires claim and color of title made in good faith, seven successive years in possession and payment of all taxes legally assessed.

A person who simply moves into a vacant house and stays does not fit that pattern. Section 13-109 is written for a claimant holding under paper title, and the owner has separate remedies against anyone entering without right.

What do the Illinois adverse possession statutes require?

Three provisions cover most Illinois cases, and each rests on time in possession.

Illinois possession statutes in Article XIII of the Code of Civil Procedure
SectionPeriodWhat the text requires
13-10120 yearsNo action to recover land or entry on it unless within 20 years after the right accrued or title or possession was acquired, except as 13-102 through 13-122 provide
13-1097 yearsActual possession under claim and color of title made in good faith, plus payment of all taxes legally assessed
13-109.12 yearsPossession by a purchaser at a judicial foreclosure sale or a buyer from the mortgagee, under a court order, plus payment of taxes

Source: 735 ILCS 5/13-101, 13-109 and 13-109.1.

Under section 13-109, a person who takes over the possession by purchase, legacy or descent before the seven years run can add that time to the earlier occupant's, so long as possession and tax payments continue. The foreclosure provision applies to actions filed 180 days or more after August 23, 2018.

What changes for Illinois heirs on January 1, 2027?

A new section, 13-109.2, created by Public Act 104-506, takes effect January 1, 2027. It lets a co-owner who inherited through intestate succession and lives in the property ask a court to be adjudged the sole owner against non-claiming relatives, if the court finds several things.

  • Each person bringing the action has household income under 80% of the area median income set by HUD for that county
  • They searched with due diligence for anyone else holding an interest
  • For 7 successive years they held exclusive possession, paid all taxes and acquired their interest through intestacy
  • For those 7 years no other tenant in common paid taxes, helped with care or upkeep, or asserted any interest

At least 2 years before suing, the claimant must record a signed declaration with the recorder of deeds and send notice to other owners by certified and first class mail, by email and text where known, and by one newspaper publication. Any owner can object by filing a signed objection with the recorder. Heirs who share an Illinois home can ask a title company how an unresolved co-owner affects a closing, and can ask the county recorder whether any declaration or objection has been filed against the parcel.

How can an Illinois owner remove someone who has no right to be there?

Illinois uses the eviction article of the Code of Civil Procedure and its criminal trespass laws. Section 9-102 lets the person entitled to possession be restored to it when a forcible entry is made, and when entry is made into vacant or unoccupied land or tenements without right or title. It also states that nothing in the article prevents law enforcement from enforcing criminal trespass under section 21-3 or from removing people or property when there is a criminal trespass.

The civil path starts in the circuit court of the county where the property sits. Under section 9-106, the owner files a complaint describing the premises and naming the defendant, and the clerk issues a summons. A complaint may not name a minor as a defendant; if it does, the whole case is dismissed and sealed. In the case, the defendant can raise any defense under a general denial, but matters not germane to possession are kept out, and a claim for rent may be joined in the complaint. When the occupant cannot be served, section 9-107 allows an affidavit and notice by posting and mailing, or by publication and mailing. The sheriff posts 3 copies of the notice in public places near the courthouse at least 10 days before the appearance date.

Is it a crime to stay in an Illinois house without permission?

It can be. Section 21-3 makes criminal trespass to real property a Class B misdemeanor when a person knowingly and without lawful authority enters or remains in a building, enters land after notice that entry is forbidden, or stays after being told to leave. Notice can be oral or written, or a printed notice posted at the main entrance. Section 19-4 separately covers criminal trespass to a residence, defined as knowingly entering or remaining without authority in a dwelling place of another.

The trespass statute does not apply to anyone living on land at the request of the owner, or under a lease or other agreement with the owner or the owner's agent. A person with a lease or permission is a tenant or guest, and removing a tenant goes through the eviction article.

  • Written notice to leave, delivered in a way you can prove
  • Photos of the property, dated, showing the condition and any unauthorized entry
  • Tax bills, deed and insurance records showing who holds title and pays
  • A police report number if a report was made

How does an occupant affect selling an Illinois property?

Document who lives in the house before listing it. If the person claims a lease, the situation is a tenancy, and section 9-102(a)(4) covers a lessee who holds possession without right after the lease ends. If the person has no right to stay, the owner can pursue the court process above and ask an Illinois attorney about timing.

The claimant under section 13-109 must show payment of the assessed taxes for the whole period, so keep the tax bills, deed and insurance records in the owner's name. Ask the circuit clerk in your county how eviction filings proceed there, and ask the sheriff's office who carries out an eviction order. A sale can close once title is clear and the occupant has left.

More questions about Illinois Squatters Rights and Adverse Possession

How long does adverse possession take in Illinois?

Seven successive years under claim and color of title made in good faith with all taxes paid, under 735 ILCS 5/13-109. A 20 year limit applies to actions to recover land under section 13-101, and a 2 year period applies to certain judicial foreclosure purchasers under 13-109.1.

Does a squatter have to pay property taxes to claim a house in Illinois?

Yes, under section 13-109 the possessor must pay all taxes legally assessed on the land for the full period. The same requirement appears in 13-109.1 and 13-109.2.

What is Illinois section 13-109.2?

A section effective January 1, 2027 that lets an heir who inherited as a tenant in common, lives in the home and meets an income test of under 80% of area median income ask a court for sole ownership after 7 years of exclusive possession and tax payment, with notice and a recorded declaration.

Can I remove an Illinois squatter myself?

Illinois provides a circuit court eviction action under Article IX and criminal trespass statutes enforced by law enforcement, and section 9-102 states that police may enforce criminal trespass. Ask an Illinois attorney or the circuit clerk before changing locks or removing belongings.

What if the occupant cannot be found to serve papers?

Section 9-107 allows constructive service on an unknown occupant by posting and mailing notices, or by publication and mailing, after the plaintiff files an affidavit that service could not be made. In that case the court may rule only on the eviction portion of the complaint.

What written notice must an Illinois landlord give before filing an eviction?

The answer depends on why the tenancy is ending. Article IX of the Code of Civil Procedure sets a different clock for unpaid rent, a broken lease term, a tenancy that simply runs out, and a handful of special situations. A landlord who picks the wrong notice or counts the days wrong can see the case thrown back before a judge reaches the real dispute.

Owners who plan to sell a house that has a tenant in it run into these rules first, because a sale contract with a delivery date only works if the tenant leaves lawfully. The main notice periods in the statute are:

  • 5 days to pay rent that is past due.
  • 10 days after a default in some other term of the lease.
  • 7 days, 30 days or 60 days to end a tenancy where nothing was breached, depending on the length of the tenancy.
  • No notice at all when a fixed lease term has expired.
  • 90 days for a bona fide lease in a home that went through foreclosure.

How many days does a rent demand give a tenant?

At least 5 days after the notice is served. Under 735 ILCS 5/9-209, a landlord may demand the rent any time after it is due and tell the tenant in writing that the lease ends unless payment arrives within the stated time. If the tenant does not pay, the landlord may treat the lease as over and file an eviction or ejectment action without any further notice or demand.

Partial payments are where these notices most often fail. The statute says payments toward the past-due rent do not invalidate the notice if they fall short of the full amount demanded, but only when the notice itself says so prominently. The required wording tells the tenant that only full payment of the rent demanded waives the right to terminate, unless the landlord agrees in writing to continue the lease for a partial payment. A notice without that sentence loses the protection.

Two more details matter in practice. A landlord who collects past rent after filing suit over the unpaid demand does not invalidate the suit. And the complaint can add a claim for the rent itself, including a prorated amount for any period when a judgment is stayed.

What notice applies when the tenant breaks a lease term other than rent?

Ten days. Section 9-210 says that once a tenant defaults in any term of the lease, the landlord needs to give no more than 10 days of notice to quit. The notice may follow the short form printed in the statute: it names the default, describes the premises, says the landlord has elected to end the lease, and tells the tenant to deliver possession within 10 days of the date. The landlord or an agent signs it, and no other demand is needed.

Typical defaults that fit here include an unauthorized occupant, a pet the lease forbids, or damage to the unit. The notice should name the actual default in plain words. A vague notice invites an argument that the tenant could not know what to fix.

How much notice ends a tenancy when nobody has defaulted?

It turns on how the tenancy is measured. The statute covers week-to-week, shorter-than-a-year, year-to-year and farm tenancies, and it says an expired fixed term needs no notice. The table lays out the periods.

Illinois notice periods when no default is claimed (Code of Civil Procedure, Article IX)
TenancyWritten noticeSection
Week to week, tenant holds over7 days9-207(a)
Term under one year, other than week to week30 days9-207(b)
Year to year60 days, given within the 4 months before the last 60 days of the year9-205
Farm land, year to yearNot less than 4 months before the end of the lease year9-206
Fixed term that has expiredNone needed9-213

Sections 9-205 and 9-207 both carry an exception for leases in foreclosed homes, covered in the next section. Month-to-month tenancies fall under the under-one-year rule, which gives the 30 day period.

Do special situations change the notice period?

Yes, and a few are worth knowing before a sale conversation starts.

  • Leases voided for crime. If a tenant or occupant uses the premises for an act that would be a felony or a Class A misdemeanor, the landlord may void the lease. If the tenant has not left within 5 days after receiving written notice to vacate, the landlord can go to court (9-120).
  • Contract purchasers and condominium owners. A demand under 9-104.1 must give at least 30 days to satisfy its terms before an action is filed.
  • Foreclosed homes with a tenant. Whoever takes control after a foreclosure, including a mortgagee, receiver or judicial sale purchaser, may end a bona fide lease only with at least 90 days of written notice (9-207.5).
  • Emergency cases. For the narrow drug, firearm or violent-crime grounds in 9-118, no predicate notice of termination is required, but the verified complaint must be served at least 14 days before the hearing.

How must the notice reach the tenant?

Section 9-211 lists the accepted ways to serve a demand or notice. A landlord may hand a written or printed copy to the tenant, or leave it with a person aged 13 or older who lives on or holds the premises. A copy can also go by certified or registered mail with a return receipt from the addressee. If no one is in actual possession, posting the notice on the premises is allowed.

Keep a dated record of how and when service happened. For a rent demand, the statute counts the 5 days from service, so leave the full period before filing. For the later court demand, 9-104 adds a path for unknown occupants who are parties to no written lease: the copy is directed to unknown occupants and delivered, left with an occupant aged 13 or older, or posted.

What does an eviction notice mean for someone selling an Illinois house?

A notice is only the first step. Until a judge enters an eviction order and the sheriff carries it out, the tenant stays lawfully in possession, and a buyer taking title cannot count on an empty house. That reality shapes how a seller prices time.

  • Check the lease for a sale clause and ask a real estate attorney whether the lease continues after closing.
  • Give the right notice for the actual reason, and keep proof of service in the file.
  • Ask the title company which documents it wants if a tenant occupies the house at closing.
  • If the house is already behind on mortgage payments, read the foreclosure rules too, since 90 day lease protection applies after a foreclosure sale.

Some owners prefer to sell the house with the tenant in place or to a buyer who purchases as-is and handles the occupancy after closing. Others negotiate a move-out date in writing. Either route is easier when the notice paperwork is clean.

Where can landlords and tenants find the court forms?

The Illinois Courts site posts approved statewide eviction forms that every circuit court must accept, and it links to a free guided interview from Illinois Legal Aid Online that fills out the complaint, the response, or a request to seal an eviction file. The same page explains that rental help through the court-based rental assistance program requires an eviction case to be on file. Visit the Illinois Courts eviction page before filing, and ask the circuit clerk in the county where the house sits about local filing steps.

More questions about Illinois Eviction Notice Rules

Is 5 days always enough notice for unpaid rent in Illinois?

Five days is the minimum the statute allows, counted from service of the written demand. The notice must also carry the full-payment warning to survive a partial payment. If the lease or a local ordinance asks for more time, the landlord should follow the longer period.

Can a landlord skip the notice when the lease term has ended?

Yes. Under section 9-213, when a tenancy for a set period expires by its own terms, the tenant must surrender possession and no notice to quit or demand is needed.

What happens if the tenant pays part of the rent after getting the notice?

The notice stays valid when the notice contains the required full-payment sentence and the payments fall short of the total demanded. Without that sentence, a partial payment can undo the notice. A landlord may also agree in writing to continue the lease in exchange for a partial payment.

How long must a landlord wait after a foreclosure to end a tenant's lease?

At least 90 days of written notice for a bona fide lease. Section 9-207.5 applies to a mortgagee, receiver, certificate holder or judicial sale purchaser who takes control of residential real estate in foreclosure. The same section keeps other termination routes in Article IX available.

Can a seller list a house while a tenant is under a termination notice?

A seller can list it, but possession is the open question until the tenant leaves or a court order is carried out. Tell the buyer and the title company about the tenancy and the notice, and have an attorney review the lease before signing a contract with a delivery date.
